title: Find duplicates in a list
instructorPromptText: Write a program that asks the user for a comma-separated list of values, then prints each value that appears more than once. Each duplicate value should be printed only once.

specGateDimensions.description: If the user types 'a, b , c,a', is the value ' b ' treated the same as 'b', or are leading/trailing spaces significant?
specGateDimensions.rationale: comma-separated input almost always contains spaces after commas; the spec must commit to stripping or not, because it changes which items count as duplicates.

specGateDimensions.description: Are 'Apple' and 'apple' considered the same value, or different values?
specGateDimensions.rationale: String equality for duplicate detection forces a commitment; students often don't notice they've implicitly chosen case-sensitive until a test surprises them.

specGateDimensions.description: In what order should the duplicates be printed — order of first appearance in the input, sorted, or unspecified?
specGateDimensions.rationale: Different data-structure choices (list vs. set vs. dict) produce different orders; forcing the commitment before coding ties the spec to the structural choice.

specGateDimensions.description: What should the program do if no value appears more than once — print nothing, print a message, or something else?
specGateDimensions.rationale: The empty-result case is almost always unstated in duplicate-finding problems and causes confused output during testing.

specGateDimensions.description: What happens if the user enters an empty string or just whitespace? Does the program assume the input is non-empty, or handle it explicitly?
specGateDimensions.rationale: Splitting an empty string yields [''], which the student may not anticipate; either handling or assuming is fine, but it must be named.

expectedDivergences.pattern: Spec commits to stripping whitespace but code uses `input().split(',')` without calling .strip() on each element, so ' apple' and 'apple' register as different
Spec says 'print each duplicate once' but code prints the duplicate every time it's encountered after the first (e.g. prints 'a' twice for input 'a,a,a')
Plan describes nested loops comparing every pair; code uses a count dictionary or a seen-set + duplicates-set pair — coherent simplification using unit_3 tools
Plan uses a dict mapping value to count; code uses two sets (seen, duplicates) — equivalent outcome, different structure
Student builds a count dict correctly but iterates the original list when printing, causing duplicates to print multiple times instead of once
Student uses `list.count(x) > 1` inside a loop over the list without tracking which values have already been printed, causing repeated output
